query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount of aluminum (~3 at.%) into equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance at elevated temperatures by promoting the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale that slows oxidation without degrading the material's room-temperature ductility or high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strengths ranging from 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with inadequate oxygen resistance leading to rapid oxidation (pesting) in air, particularly around 800 °C.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying addition of aluminum (approximately 3 atomic percent) to the base equiatomic alloy.
generation.conditions: Oxidation testing in air at 800 °C for an exposure time of 5 hours, with mechanical property assessments performed under conditions similar to those originally reported (room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength tests at strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, continuous, and adherent Al2O3 oxide scale on the material’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The added Al preferentially oxidizes at the high-temperature surface, yielding a stable Al2O3 film. This film acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen ingress, significantly reducing the rate of oxidation of the underlying metal matrix. The intervention aims to achieve this improved oxidation resistance while maintaining the advantageous mechanical properties of the original alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-alloyed HfNbTaTiZr is expected to exhibit a substantially lower weight gain (indicative of reduced oxidation) and formation of a protective Al2O3 layer compared to the untreated alloy, with retention of its useful room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr shows inadequate oxygen resistance at elevated temperatures (e.g., rapid oxidation or pesting during a 5 h air exposure at 800 °C) despite its favorable mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis specifically applies to short-term (5-hour) high-temperature (around 800 °C) oxidation in air. The long-term oxidation behavior, performance under more aggressive mechanical loading, and potential changes in microstructure at other temperatures constitute areas of uncertainty.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal aluminum concentration and its effect on the alloy’s microstructure may vary; even a small Al addition might slightly alter mechanical properties or phase stability. Additionally, while the beneficial effect of Al in forming protective oxide scales is well established in other systems, its exact efficacy in this specific equiatomic refractory alloy needs to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the standard equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr, and another set with ~3 at.% aluminum added. Expose both sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. Following the exposure, conduct weight gain measurements, surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (using SEM, TEM, and XRD to identify oxide phases), and evaluate mechanical properties (room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength) to compare the oxidation behavior and mechanical performance.
measurements: Oxide layer morphology and continuity (via SEM/TEM imaging)
Phase identification of the oxide layer (via XRD)
High-temperature yield strength at 1000 °C under controlled strain rates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-alloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (lower weight gain and absence of discontinuous or porous oxide scales) compared to the untreated samples, or if the protective oxide scale does not predominantly consist of Al2O3, or if the mechanical properties (ductility and yield strength) are compromised beyond acceptable limits, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
